title: CRLA/667/2019 of P D RAM Vs C.B.I.S.P.E. DEHRADUN

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 667 of 2019
P.D. Ram ........... Appellant
Vs.
Central Bureau of Investigation ........ Respondent
Present : Mr. Harshit Sanwal, learned Amicus Curiae.
 Mr. Sandeep Tandon, Advocate for the CBI.

JUDGMENT
Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J. (Oral)
Present appeal is preferred against the
judgment and order dated 12.01.2000, passed in CBI
Case No. 3 of 1998, CBI Vs. Kesar Chand & others, by the
Court of Special Judge, Anti Corruption, U.P. (East),
Dehradun. By the impugned judgment and order the
appellant has been convicted under Section 120-B read
with 420 IPC, Section 13 (2) read with Section 13 (1) (d) of
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 ("the Act") and
Section 109 read with 420, Section 471 read with 468,
Section 467 read with 468 IPC and sentenced as
hereunder:-

2
(i) Under Section 120-B IPC to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of two
years and a fine of Rs.2500/-.
(ii) Under Section 109 IPC to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of two
years and a fine of Rs.2500/-.
(iii) Under Section 467 IPC to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of two
years and a fine of Rs.2500/-.
(iv) Under Section 468 IPC to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of two
years and a fine of Rs.2500/-.
(v) Under Section 471 IPC to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for a period of two
years and a fine of Rs.2500/-.
(vi) Under Section 13 (2) of the Act to
undergo rigorous imprisonment for a
period of two years and a fine of
Rs.2500/-
2. The case is based on an FIR lodged by Arjun
Singh Somwanshi, Assistant Divisional Account Officer,
Railway on 06.01.1994 against the appellant and others,
under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 IPC at Police Station
Civil Lines, Sadar, District Moradabad.

3
3. The prosecution case, briefly stated, is as
follows:-
The appellant P.D. Ram was working in his
capacity as Assistant Divisional Account Officer (A.D.A.O),
Divisional Accounts Office, Northern Railway, Muradabad.
The co-convict Keshar Chand was working as Dealing
Assistant in the same section and co-convict Kishan Lal
was Senior Section Officer posted with them. The
Northern Railways had awarded contract of loading and
erecting slabs to a Ravi Verma Prabhakar, Contractor on
17.09.1993. An agreement No. 51/DRM/M.D. (for short,
"the agreement") dated 17.09.1993 was executed between
the Northern Railways and Ravi Verma Prabhakar.
According to the prosecution, on 15.10.1993 and
12.11.1993, two forged bills were prepared with regard to
the agreement by the appellant and other co-convicts for
Rs.8,66,695/- and Rs.8,99,140/- respectively. Based on
the forged bill, cheques were obtained in the name of the
Contractor by Keshav Chand, Dealing Assistant. Keshav
Chand, Dealing Assistant also opened a forged account
in the name of Ravi Verma Prabhakar, the Contractor, in
the State Bank of India, Civil Lines Moradabad and
deposited the cheque in that account.

4
4. The matter was transferred to the Central Bureau of
Investigation ("CBI") the matter was investigated, various
documents were taken in to custody by the Investigating
Officer ("IO"). The IO also took specimen signatures and
handwritings of various persons for expert opinion. After
investigation, the IO submitted the charge sheet against
the appellant and others for the offences punishable
under Sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471, 477A 201 IPC
and Section 13 (2) read with Section 13 (1) (d) of the Act.
On 14.11.1998, charge under Sections 120B read with
420 IPC and Section 13 (2) read with Section 13 (1) (d) of
the Act and Section 109 read with 420, Section 471 read
with 468, Section 467, 468 IPC and 13(2) read 13 (1) (d) of
the Act were framed against the appellant. The appellant
denied the charges and claimed trial.
5. Prosecution, in order to prove the case,
examined 16 witnesses, namely, PW1 A.K. Basu, PW2
P.C. Singh, PW3 M.S. Sinha, PW4 Digvijay Singh, PW5
Umesh Chandra Saxena, PW6 Fazal Mohmmad, PW7 R.P.
Mishra, PW8 A.A. Abbasi, PW9 D.P. Sharma, PW10
Surendra Kumar Sharma, PW11 Mangat Singh, PW12
Rakesh Kumar Verma, PW13 Dr. S.C. Mittal, PW14 B.S.

5
Pangti, PW15 Rakesh Kumar Chauhan and PW16
Pashupal Singh.
6. After prosecution evidence, the appellant was
examined under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 ("the Code"). According to him, he has
been falsely implicated.
7. The appellant in his statement under Section
313 of the Code has stated that the bills were on account
bills. Such bills were not checked by the A.D.A.O. He
merely signed on the bills. He had no knowledge that the
bills were forged. According to the appellant, he did
everything in accordance with the rules. He has been an
officer of unblemished record. He could not think of
committing such act, at the verge of his retirement.
8. The court below, after hearing the parties,
convicted and sentenced the appellant and others.
Aggrieved by it, the appellant has challenged his
conviction and sentence in the instant appeal.
9. Heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the record.

6
10. Learned amicus curiae would submit that the
prosecution has utterly failed to prove the case against
the appellant. The appellant ought to have been acquitted
of the charge. The court below committed gross error in
convicting and sentencing the appellant. The following
points have also been raised in his submissions by the
learned amicus curiae:-
(i) There is no evidence as to where the
money withdrawn from the Government
account had gone.
(ii) As per FIR, information was received with
regard to the forged bills from the
Engineering Department. Whereas, the
evidence speaks otherwise.
(iii) Even, the bills in question have not been
produced before the court. Certain pages
are missing
(iv) The bills in question were received from
the Engineering Branch as proved by
PW15 Rakesh Kumar Chauhan.
(v) Prosecution has not proved that the
petitioner has committed any wrong.

7
(vi) The bills in question were duly filled up.
There were signatures and stamps at
appropriate places.
(vii) The appellant did not have any idea that
any signature or stamp was forged on the
bills.
(viii) The appellant was not required to check
the bill details. It was the duty of the
Dealing Assistant and the Senior Section
Officer.
(ix) The measurement book which is recorded
in the bill in question as well as the ledger
book has not been produced by the
prosecution.
(x) It is not the case of the prosecution that
in any manner, the appellant has been
benefitted by any misdeed.
11. On the other hand, learned counsel for
the CBI would submit that under the conspiracy, the
appellant alongwith other co-convicts forged the
documents and misappropriated the Government
money. He would raise the following points in his
submissions:-

8
(i) Admittedly, the bills were forged and total
amount of bills were exceeding the total
amount involved in the agreement.
(ii) Signatures on the bills were forged.
(iii) Had the appellant been little more careful,
the offence could not have been
committed. In fact, it is argued that
without connivance or conspiracy with the
appellant such forgery could not have
been committed.
(iv) The design of the appellant to commit the
crime is evident that he deputed PW4
Digvijay Singh to prepare a cheque on the
date when the cheque writer was on leave.
PW4 Digvijay Singh was totally new to the
such assignment and it was so done by
the appellant under a design. The
witnesses have proved that the entries in
the bills in question were forged, false.
The date of agreement was wrongly
written in such bills.
(v) The prosecution could not have produced
any MB because for the work in question

9
MB had even not been issued when the
bills were prepared because the work did
not commence till then.
12. Learned counsel for the CBI would submit that
the Court below did not commit any error in convicting
and sentencing the appellant. Therefore, the appeal is
devoid of merits.
13. PW1 A.K. Basu was the Joint Secretary,
Establishment, Railway Board, New Delhi. He accorded
the prosecution sanction to prosecute the appellant. He
has proved the sanction.
14. PW2 P.C. Singh had accorded sanction to
prosecute co-accused Umesh Chand.
15. PW3 M. S. Sinha, accorded prosecution
sanction against co-convict Kesar Chand.
16. PW4 Digvijay Singh, was working at the
Divisional Account Office, Moradabad at the relevant
time. According to him, on 15.01.1993, M.P. Saxena, the
cheque writer was on leave. Therefore, the appellant
deputed this witness to perform the duties of cheque
writer. He issued a cheque for Rs. 8,66,695/-. The

10
witness has proved the cheque and its entry in register
CO-7, which is prepared once bills are cleared. This
witness has also proved entries made on register CO-7 by
the appellant.
17. PW5 Umesh Chandra Saxena was working as
Senior Account Officer at the relevant time in Moradabad.
He has stated about the procedure for processing the
claims of the contract. According to him, the procedure is
as follows:-
(i) The bills are received from Engineering
Branch to the Account Section.
(ii) The Account Section enters them in a
register CO-6.
(iii) CO-6 register is maintained on monthly
basis.
(iv) After entry in the register CO-6, the bill is
assigned to the Dealing Assistant
alongwith measurement book.
(v) The Dealing Assistant makes his
signatures in the register CO-6 and
acknowledges the receipt of the bills.

11
(vi) the Dealing Assistant checks the entries
in the bills alongwith measurement book
and agreement/work order. He satisfies
himself that claims made in the bills are
in accordance with the agreement or work
order. He also satisfies that the
arithmetical calculations and
measurements, as recorded in the
measurement book are correct.
(vii) Thereafter, Dealing Assistant makes entry
in the contract ledger and forward them to
the Section Officer.
(viii) The Section Officer again checks the bills
and makes his signature. Thereafter, the
bills are send to A.D.A.O., who makes his
signatures in the bills, measurement book
and ledger book and returns it to the
Dealing Assistant.
(ix) The Dealing Assistant thereafter makes
entries in the register CO-7 (extract of
bills) and forwards it to the Section Officer
under his signatures.

12
(xi) The Section Officer thereafter tallies the
entries in register CO-7 and makes his
signatures on it and forwards it to the
A.D.A.O.
(xii) The A.D.A.O. after signing register CO-7
forwards it to the cheque writer and
thereafter, cheques are made and they are
forwarded to the Contractor either by post
or are given to him, if the Contractor is
personally present and identified.
18. This witness has stated about the whole
procedure. This witness has also about some documents
which he had given to the IO and proved them.
19. PW6 Fazal Mohammad has stated that on
18.10.1993, co-convict Kesar Chand met him in the State
Bank of India, Civil Lines Branch, Moradabad and
requested him to introduce a person as Ravi Verma
Prabhakar. Therefore, he introduced him and an account
of Ravi Verma Prabhakar was opened. According to this
witness, subsequently, he came to know that Kesar
Chand had got wrong man introduced by him. He has
proved his signatures in the proforma, by which, he
introduced Ravi Verma Prabhakar.

13
20. PW7 R.P. Mishra, is the Engineer, who
executed the agreement with Ravi Verma Prabhakar,
Contractor. He has proved the agreement. According to
this witness, Bill No. 117/A.E.N./CH amounting to
Rs.866,695/- was not processed from their department
and the signatures on this bill are forged. He has also
stated about the bill amounting to Rs. 8,99,140/- and
stated that it is also forged. PW7 R.P. Mishra has also
stated that first on account bill, under the agreement, for
Rs.2,26,076/-, was prepared, but it could not be passed.
21. PW8 A.A. Abbasi, has prepared the cheque for
the second bill for Rs.8,99,140/-. He proved the cheque.
According to him, he had verified register CO-7 before
preparing the cheque.
22. PW9 D.P. Sharma was working with the
Engineer Department of the Railway at the relevant time.
He has stated about the agreement and the on account
bill for Rs.2,26,076/-. According to him, the forged bills
were not originated from their branch. According to him,
the contact number was also wrongly mentioned in both
the forged bills.

14
23. PW10 Surendra Kumar Sharma has also stated
about the agreement entered in between the railways and
Ravi Verma Prabhakar. According to him, with regard to
the agreement, the security was not entered in the
relevant register after the bills were prepared. Therefore,
he summoned the document from co-convict Kesar Chand
and directed him to make entry in the security register.
According to PW10 Surendra Kumar Sharma, co-convict
did not return him those bills and when he inquired
about it, they were not traceable. This witness has stated
quite in detail that subsequently, he came to know that
the bills were forged. He has also stated that the Dealing
Assistant, Kesar Chand was custodian of agreement,
Contract Ledger and measurement book. After clearance
of the bills, according to this witness, the measurement
book should have been returned to the executive side. He
has identified the signatures of the appellant in the bills
in question. According to him, these bills were filled up by
co-convict Kesar Chand. He has identified the
handwriting of Kesar Chand and exhibited the documents
accordingly. PW10 Surendra Kumar Sharma would state
that in both the bills first on account bill was also
wrongly recorded. This witness has also stated about the
role of other co-convicts.

15
24. PW11 Mangat Singh was working In-Charge of
Works, Chandausi, District Moradabad at the relevant
time. According to him, the agreement with Ravi Verma
Prabhakar was executed on 17.09.1993. The total cost of
the work is Rs.933500/- According to him, both the bills
were not processed from their department and they were
not signed by the person, who were required to sign on
those bills.
25. PW12 Rakesh Kumar Verma has also stated
about the agreement executed between Railways and Ravi
Verma Prabhakar.
26. PW13 Dr. S.C. Mittal is a Senior Scientific
Officer, Grade-1, in the Central Forensic Laboratory. He
submitted his report after examination of the documents.
He has proved the report Ex. A27.
27. PW14 B.S. Pangti, is Senior Officer, SBI.
According to him, he had allowed for opening of the
account of Ravi Verma Prabhakar on 18.10.1993, which
was introduced by one of the employees of the bank
Umesh Chandra.
28. PW15 Rakesh Kumar Chauhan is the person,
who was assigned the duty to receive bills from Accounts

16
Section and make entries in CO-6 register. According to
him, the bills in question were entered in CO-6 register
and he had marked "K.C." on it.
29. PW16 Pashupal Singh is the Investigating
Officer. He has stated about the steps which he has taken
during investigation.
30. In this appeal, the Court is concerned about
the role of appellant P.D. Ram alone. During the course of
hearing, CO-6 register maintained in the Accounts branch
of railways has been perused by the Court. In fact, PW15
Rakesh Kumar Chauhan has stated about it. According to
him, in pages 31 and 61 of the CO-6 register, entries with
regard to the bills in question have been made and he has
marked "K.C." on it. A perusal of this register reveals that
"K.C." has been marked on a column no.7, which relates
to initials of the Clerk receiving the bill.. Does it relates to
Kesar Chand, the Dealing Assistant? Who, in fact,
according to the prosecution, is the person working as the
Dealing Assistant in the Account Section. If it is so, does
it mean that the bills were entered into the register CO-6
by PW15 Rakesh Kumar Chauhan and he marked both
the bills to the Dealing Assistant, Kesar Chand. If it is so,
the question is who forwarded those bills to the Accounts

17
Section. This cloud is not clear. There is immense doubt
on it.
31. It is not in dispute that the bills were forged.
Prosecution has led evidence that the bills were prepared
in the handwriting of co-convict Kesar Chand. In fact, in
his examination under Section 313 of the Code, co-convict Kesar Chand has admitted his role. Though, he
has stated that he was given blank bills by Senior Section
Officer, co-convict Kishan Lal and the signatures etc. were
done at the residence of the appellant. It is important to
notice that in page 37 of the impugned judgment in para
2, the court had taken note of the statement of the co-convict Kesar Chand recorded under Section 313 of the
Code.
32. The statement recorded under Section 313 of
the Code of an accused itself is not substantive evidence.
It may not be the basis for convicting a person. A
conviction cannot be based on any statement given under
Section 313 of the Code. The statement of the co-accused
is more weak kind of such statement.
33. PW5 Umesh Chand Saxena has submitted in
detail about the procedure. He has been categorical that

18
the Dealing Assistant has to verify the bills with the
agreement, with the measurement book with regard to the
measurements and arithmetical calculations. Thereafter,
enter it in the ledger book and sign on it and forward it to
the Senior Section Officer. According to PW5 Umesh
Chand Saxena, the same procedure has to be adopted by
the Senior Section Officer (Statement of PW5 Umesh
Chand Saxena, page 2) but at Page 3, top line, PW5
Umesh Chand Saxena has stated that A.D.A.O. only
makes his signatures in the bills, measurement book and
the ledger and returns it to the Dealing Assistant.
34. When asked that A.D.A.O. is required to check
only 2 % of the entries, PW5 Umesh Chand Saxena could
not reveal anything exactly on this point (statement of
PW5 page 11). Though, he would submit that specific
duties of the officers, in the Accounts Section may find
place in Engineering Code, Accounts Code or General
Code. Interestingly, the prosecution has not proved any
such document to establish that as per the working
procedure, the A.D.A.O was required to look into certain
documents? There is no evidence to that effect, as to what
was required to be checked by the appellant before
making his signatures on the bills in question.

19
35. In fact, there has always been a line between
dereliction of duties and commission of offence. An officer
in the Government department may be hugely careless in
discharge of his duties and may thereby cause losses to
the public exchequer, but every such action may not be
termed as a criminal offence. Criminality is something
different than dereliction or negligence in discharge of the
duties. This line is required to be cleared by the
prosecution in order to establish that the carelessness or
negligence of the officer was with a design to commit an
offence.
36. The Court is proceeding to examine that
aspect. Because, undoubtedly, according to the evidence
adduced by the prosecution, the total cost of the work
under the agreement was Rs.9,33,500/- and the
agreement was executed on 17.09.1993. Just one month
thereafter, on 15.10.1993, a running bill for Rs.8,66695/-
and on 12.11.1993 another bill for Rs.8,99,140/- were
cleared. It reveals that there was gross negligence even on
the part of the appellant. If the standing procedure in the
Accounts section of the Railway, Moradabad does not
require that the agreement has to be seen by such
Officers, who finally clears the bill, it may be a fault of

20
such procedure. Importantly, the bills in question have
not been produced in full before the Court. There are
certain pages missing in it.
37. Witnesses have revealed it, that the bills are
made in multiple copies. In fact, PW7 R.P. Mishra, would
state that the bills are prepared in four copies. Whereas,
PW11 Mangat Singh would also tell that it was prepared
in four copies. Although, PW5 Umesh Chand Saxena has
stated that the bills are prepared in triplicate. Be it as it
may, where are those bills? Not even a single bill in
complete has been filed. Why is it so?
38. It is the case of the prosecution that once the
bills are received by the Dealing Assistant. He checks it
with the measurement book and with the agreement in all
respect and he enters into the contract ledger. Where is
that ledger? PW10 Surendra Kumar Sharma, at page 12,
para 2 of his statement would submit that the Contractor
ledger was not seized and he also did not get a copy of the
Contractor ledger. Although, on the bottom para on the
same page, he would submit that the Contractor ledger
for the years 1992 and 1993 were seized. Where are those
ledgers? They have not been proved. Had the Dealing
Assistant made any entry in the Contract ledger with

21
regard to the bills in question? Had the appellant signed
on it? Or who had filled up the ledger book if it was ever
filled up? The prosecution has not produced even single
evidence to prove it.
39. Learned counsel for the CBI would submit that
at least the appellant could have seen the agreement or
the measurement book. The question is as to what was
produced before the appellant at the time when he signed
those bills? Both the bills records number of
measurement book ("MB")in it. Bill dated 15.10.1993 has
recorded Measurement Book No. 184 of 1992 on it. Bill
dated 12.11.1993 has recorded MB No.35 of 1992 on it.
As stated, PW7 R.P. Mishra in page 4 of his statement
would tell that MB for that work was not ever issued.
PW11 Mangat Singh in page 6 of his statement would
submit that MB Nos. 184 of 1992 and 35 of 1992 were
never issued from their office. This witness has stated
that movement register is though maintained in their
office. What is interesting to note is that PW12 Rakesh
Kumar Verma has categorically stated that MB No. 184 of
1992 and 35 of 1992 belong to their office (statement of
PW12 Rakesh Kumar Verma, page 4 bottom and page 5
first para). According to this witness, these measurement

22
books were forwarded to the Accounts Section but these
were not brought back despite repeated requests, oral as
well as in writing. The witnesses have spoken about the
movement register of the measurement book.
40. The prosecution did not produce MB Nos.184
of 1992 and 35 of 1992. Why? Their production could
have cleared the doubt about the work measured under
the measurement books. The movement register would
have cleared the doubts as to whether such MBs were
forwarded to the Accounts Branch or not. As stated
hereinbefore, the CO-6 register maintained by PW15
Rakesh Kumar Chauhan had made entry with regard to
both the bills on those registers and in the relevant
column it has also been marked that the bills were given
for further processing to the Dealing Assistant marked as
"K.C.". Had Accounts Branch also received the
measurement book alongwith those bills? It is not clear. It
is all in doubt.
41. At this stage, the Court would like to note that,
in fact, PW15 Rakesh Kumar Chauhan has not stated in
his examination-in-chief, as to who made entry, with
regard to the bills, in CO-6 register. This witness, during
investigation, had told it to the IO that this entry was

23
made by Kesar Chand. The IO has also confirmed it. This
Court has not examined the role of co-convict Kesar
Chand. Had the bills been prepared by the co-convict
Kesar Chand and he made entry in CO6 register on his
own handwriting or he forged the MB 184/92 and 32/92?
Did he forged the ledger book also? and Did he place
those documents before the appellant for his signatures
after due verification by the Senior Section Officer, Kishan
Lal? It is not clear. And if it is done so, what is the role of
the appellant? How can it be said that the appellant
conspired with other co-convicts to commit the crime? He
did not forge the bills. He has not filled up those forms
and bills. The prosecution has not proved that it was the
duty of the appellant under the rules to check certain
entries which he did not. Moreover, as stated mere
dereliction of duties and carelessness does not amount to
an offence.
42. According to the prosecution, the cheques were
received by Kesar Chand and it is co-convict Kesar Chand
who opened a forged account in the SBI, Civil Lines,
Sadar Branch, Moradabad and he issued cheque from
that account also. But, it is not the prosecution case that
any money from that account or any proceed of this
crime, in any manner, was taken by the appellant.

24
43. On behalf of the CBI, it is argued that under a
design the appellant deputed PW4 Digvijai Singh as
cheque writer when the regular employee was on leave.
This argument has no merit for acceptance. If one cheque
was made by PW4 Digvijai Singh, there was another
cheque also. It is not a case that the appellant did
anything discreetly. Merely because PW4 Digvijai Singh
was deputed one day as Cheque Writer, it does not
attribute any criminal intent or design to the appellant.
44. In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court
is of the view that, in fact, prosecution has utterly failed
to prove the charges against the appellant. Accordingly,
the appeal deserves to be allowed.
45. The appeal is allowed.
46. The impugned judgment and order in so far it
convicts and sentences the appellant is set aside. The
appellant P.D.Ram is acquitted of the charge under
Section 120-B, 109, 467, 468, 471 IPC and Section 13 (2)
of the Act.
47. Appellant is on bail. His bonds cancelled and
sureties are discharged of their liability.

25
48. Let a copy of this judgment along with Lower
Court Record be forwarded to the Court below for
compliance.
 (Ravindra Maithani, J.)
 30.12.2021 Jitendra
